sec.title: Background
sec.p: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is one of the most common malignant tumors. Although several treatments have been proposed, the long-term prognosis of this cancer is poor. Lipid droplets and mitochondria are important organelles that regulate energy metabolism in cells and are postulated to promote the occurrence and progression of tumors. However, few risk prediction models have been constructed based on lipid drop-mitochondria-related genes (LMRGs).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In this study, we constructed a lipid drop-mitochondrial (LD-M) risk score model based on data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) databases. Biological functions and clinical benefits associated with the various risk scores were analyzed using R software, GraphPad Prism 9, and the online database system.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: An LD-M risk score model comprising ABLIM3, AK4, CAV2, CPS1, CYP24A1, DLGAP5, FGR, and SH3BP5, was developed and its predictive power was validated. The risk score was closely associated with the cell cycle. Immunophenoscore (IPS) and Tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion (TIDE) results demonstrated that the low-risk group was more sensitive to immunotherapy. Drug sensitivity analysis indicated that BMS-754807, ZM447439, SB216763, and other drugs had lower IC50 values in the low-risk group.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Our results suggest that the LD-M risk score is an effective prognostic indicator for individualized treatment of LUAD.
Keywords: Lung adenocarcinoma, Lipid droplets, Mitochondria, Immunotherapy, Drug sensitivity

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: According to the data released by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), although the incidence rate of lung cancer has dropped from first place to the second-most common cancer, it remains the main cause of cancer-related deaths [1, 2]. In 2020, it was estimated that 1.8 million people died of lung cancer worldwide, far exceeding that of other cancer types [1]. A global study on the histological subtypes of lung cancer reported that in 2020, adenocarcinoma was the most common subtype of lung cancer worldwide [2]. Among 2,206,771 new cases of lung cancer, male and female adenocarcinomas accounted for 39% and 57%, respectively [2]. In recent years, despite the emergence of new therapeutic drugs and comprehensive treatments, the overall prognosis of lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) has not significantly improved [3, 4].

Mitochondria are important players in cellular metabolism, including in tumor cells [5]. They not only provide the energy needed to sustain the growth of tumors (migration and survival) but also provide energy for the reprogramming of tumor metabolites and genes [6, 7]. Mutations of mitochondrial genes contribute to the initiation of LUAD [8, 9]. Therefore, drugs targeting mitochondria are considered to be potential treatments for tumors [6].

Lipid droplets, which have long been regarded as simple cytoplasmic lipid encapsulations or inert cellular substances called triglycerides, have been recently found to actively shuttle between various organelles and transmit energy [10–13]. Moreover, the lipid droplets contribute to the initiation of various diseases, including cancer [13–15]. Accumulation of lipid droplets has been documented in various tumor tissues, and these lipid droplets supply the energy required for tumor proliferation, migration, and survival [16–18]. This implies that targeting lipid droplets may be an effective approach for treating tumors [11, 14].

In addition, a recent study on mitochondria in LUAD and squamous cell carcinoma found that mitochondria influence the accumulation of lipid droplets, producing unique subcellular structures that support the tumor's cellular metabolism and mitochondrial activity [19]. Based on this finding, we aimed to explore the key lipid droplet-mitochondrial-related genes (LMRGs) involved in LUAD and establish a prediction model for LUAD.

sec.title: Data source
sec.p: The training data were derived from the RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data of LUAD in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database (https://www.cancer.gov/tcga), comprising 600 samples derived from 517 LUAD patients. The 600 samples included 541 tumor tissues and 59 adjacent cancer tissues. The validation data, GSE31210, was obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/), and comprised lung tissue samples from 226 LUAD patients and 20 healthy individuals. In the subsequent survival-related analysis process, patients with missing survival data and an overall survival time (OS) of 0 were excluded. Lipid droplet gene set was derived from the Lipid Droplet Knowledge Portal (LDKP, https://lipiddroplet.org/) [20]. The Mitochondrial gene set was derived from the MitoCarta 3.0 database (https://www.broadinstitute.org/mitocarta/mitocarta30-inventory-mammalian-mitochondrial-proteins-and-pathways) [21] and the Gene set enrichment analyses (GSEA, http://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/index.jsp) [22]. The cell cycle gene set was retrieved from the GSEA database [22].

sec.title: Identification of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and the key lipid droplet-mitochondria-related genes (LMRGs)
sec.p: The “limma” package of R 4.3.1 was used to identify DEGs between the normal group and the tumor group, and the different risk groups. The criteria for screening DEGs were |log 2 (fold change)|> 1 and adjusted p< 0.05. The “ggplot2” package was used to construct volcano plots to display the DEGs. The common genes among lipid droplet (LD) genes, mitochondrial genes, and DEGs in the normal and tumor groups were illustrated through Venn diagrams. Subsequently, the key LMRGs were further identified from the common genes using univariate COX, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression, and multivariate COX.

The receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) curve and the area under the curve (AUC) were analyzed to assess the predictive power of the LD-M risk model.

sec.title: Kyoto encyclopedia of genes and genomes (KEGG) and gene ontology (GO)
sec.p: The “clusterProfiler”, “org.Hs.eg.db”, “enrichplot”, and “ggplot2” packages in the R 4.3.1 software were utilized to perform KEGG and GO analyses for the identified DEGs in the high and low-risk groups. Significant functional enrichment was selected based on the p< 0.05.

sec.title: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)
sec.p: The GSEA analysis of DEGs in the high and low-risk groups was performed using the “limma”, “org.Hs.eg.db”, “clusterProfiler”, and “enrichplot” packages in the R 4.3.1, software and the “c2.cp.kegg_legacy.v2023.2.Hs.symbols” from the GSEA database (http://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/index.jsp) [22] served as the target gene set for the analysis. It provided secondary verification of the above KEGG enrichment analysis results. The adjusted p < 0.05 served as the screening criteria.

sec.title: Gene set variation analysis (GSVA)
sec.p: Functional enrichment scoring for each sample in the high and low-risk groups was performed in the “GSVA” package of R 4.3.1 using the cell cycle gene list from the GSEA database (http://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/index.jsp) [22]. The enrichment results were displayed on a heatmap constructed using the “pheatmap” package of R 4.3.1, and the correlation between the risk score and the enriched cell cycle items was analyzed by Pearson correlation.

sec.title: Immunophenoscore (IPS)
sec.p: Initially, IPS analysis was performed on the training set data using The Cancer Immunome Atlas (TCIA, https://tcia.at/home) [24, 25]. Subsequently, the Immuno-Oncology Biological Research (IOBR) package in R 4.3.1 was used to separately calculate the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules, effector cells (EC), suppressor cells (SC), checkpoints (CP), averaged z-score (AZ), and IPS in the training and validation sets.

sec.title: Tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion (TIDE)
sec.p: To further investigate the response of patients in different risk groups to immunotherapy, the tumor immune escape capacity was explored on the TIDE (http://tide.dfci.harvard.edu/) [26, 27], and results were displayed by violin plots using the ggplot2 package of R 4.3.1.

sec.title: Immune infiltration analysis
sec.p: Using the “CIBERSORT” package in R 4.3.1, we conducted immune infiltration analysis on patients in the high and low-risk groups. Next, we performed Pearson correlation analysis to determine the correlation between the risk score and the common immune checkpoints [28]. The “ggplot2” package in R 4.3.1 was employed to draw boxplots and visualize the immune infiltration and the expression level of common immune checkpoints in various risk groups.

sec.title: Drug sensitivity analysis
sec.p: The half maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of 198 antitumor compounds derived from the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC, https://www.cancerrxgene.org/) [29] were calculated using the “oncoPredict” package of R 4.3.1 to explore the sensitivity of patients in different risk groups to antitumor compounds.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were conducted using the R 4.3.1 and GraphPad Prism 9 software. Data that followed normal distribution were compared using the Student’s t-test between the two groups, otherwise, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used. In addition, the Pearson correlation analysis was employed to conduct correlation analysis. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Determination of the key LMRGs in LUAD
sec.p: Differential analysis of genes in normal and LUAD tissues derived from the TCGA LUAD data identified 1981 DEGs (Fig. 1a). The intersection of these genes with 1,9199 LD genes and 2030 mitochondrial genes resulted in 142 LMRGs in lung adenocarcinoma (Fig. 1b). Next, we performed a univariate COX regression analysis on the 142 LMRGs and identified 22 potential risk factors associated with the prognosis of LUAD patients (Fig. 1c). The number of genes was reduced to 16 in the LASSO regression analysis, and further to 8 in the multivariate COX regression analysis (Fig. 1d, e). The expression profile of the 8 key LMRGs between the normal and tumor groups is presented in (Fig. 1f). Notably, ABLIM3, CAV2, FGR, and SH3BP5 were overexpressed in normal tissues, while AK4, CPS1, CYP24A1, and DLGAP5 were upregulated in the tumor tissues. The detailed information of the 8 LMRGs is shown in Table 1.

Blue dots represent genes down-regulated versus the normal group and red dots represent genes up-regulated. b Venn diagram of 1981 DEGs with 19,199 LD genes and 2,030 mitochondria genes. The intersection of the three displays 142 LMGs. c 22 LUAD potential risk genes derived from COX univariate analysis of 142 LMGs. d 16 LMGs were obtained from further lasso regression of 22 LUAD potential risk genes. e 8 key LMGs were obtained from multivariate COX regression of 16 LMGs. f Expression of 8 key LMGs in normal and tumor groups. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was applied to compare the two groups, and p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant

The survival time, status, gender, age, smoking history of the patients, and the expression of 8 key LMGs in the high and low-risk groups are presented in Figs. 2a and b. Kaplan–Meier survival analysis for both the training and validation cohorts revealed significantly poorer overall survival in the high-risk group compared to the low-risk group (p< 0.05, Fig. 2c, d). To evaluate the predictive accuracy of the risk score model for the 1-year, 2-year, 3-year, 4-year, and 5-year OS, we calculated the AUC value. sec.title: Expression of 8 key LMGs’ in the high and low-risk groups
sec.p: In further analyses, we compared the expression levels of eight key LMGs across various risk groups. In the training cohort, all LMGs, except for CAV2, demonstrated significant differences in expression. Specifically, ABLIM3, AK4, CPS1, CYP24A1, and DLGAP5 were significantly upregulated in the high-risk group, while FGR and SH3BP5 were downregulated (Fig. 3a). In the validation group, except for CPS1, the expression levels of the remaining LMGs showed significant differences between the groups, following a trend consistent with that observed in the training group (Fig. 3b).

caption.p: The expression of 8 key LMGs in the different risk groups. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was applied to compare the two groups, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant

sec.title: The risk score is closely correlated with the cell cycle mediated by chromosomal mitosis
sec.p: To identify the biological functions and pathways associated with the risk score, we performed a differential analysis between high-risk and low-risk groups, followed by KEGG, GO, and GSEA on the DEGs. In the training group, the KEGG and GO analyses indicated that the risk score was potentially associated with the cell cycle mediated by chromosomal mitosis (Fig. 4a, b). Similar results were obtained in the validation group (Fig. 4c, d). Furthermore, the GSEA revealed enrichment of the cell cycle gene set in the high-risk group (Fig. 4e, f).

caption.p: Enrichment analysis of DEGs in the different risk groups. a, c KEGG analysis of DEGs in the different risk score groups. b, d GO analysis of DEGs in the different groups. e, f GSEA analysis identified different gene sets in the high-risk group

sec.title: The risk score is positively correlated with the cell cycle
sec.p: We further calculated the enrichment scores of the risk score with 101 cell cycle-related gene sets through GSVA analysis. Subsequently, the Pearson correlation analysis was performed to determine the relationship between the risk score and the cell cycle gene set. A total of 80 cell cycle genes were found to be positively correlated and 11 were negatively correlated with the risk score in the training group. In comparison, 64 and 21 cell cycle genes were positively and negatively correlated with the risk scores, respectively, in the validation group. The top 10 most relevant cell cycle gene sets were positively correlated with the risk score (Fig. 5a, b).

Samples were sorted in ascending order according to risk score. The right column graph and line graph represented the R-value and p-value of the correlation analysis, respectively. The enrichment score was obtained using GSVA analysis. The Pearson correlation analysis was employed for correlation analysis

sec.title: The risk score can assist in the prediction of the immunogenicity and response of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) of LAUD
sec.p: To investigate the relationship between the risk score and immunogenicity of LUAD, we calculated the IPS for the high and low-risk groups. Using the TCIA database (https://tcia.at/home), we assessed the sensitivity of the training group to cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen-4 (CTLA-4) and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) immune inhibitors. The findings revealed that the IPS scores for the low-risk group were significantly higher than those for the high-risk group (Fig. 6a). The IOBR analysis further supported these results, showing that the total IPS and AZ scores were consistently higher in the low-risk group than in the high-risk group, across both the training and validation cohorts. For the training group, among the individual IPS scores, EC and CP were not significantly different between the low- and high-risk groups, while the MHC score was significantly higher in the low-risk group, and the SC score showed the opposite results. These results were not obtained in the validation group (Fig. 6b, c). Further, we conducted a TIDE analysis to examine the immune escape capacity of different risk groups. Results indicated that the total TIDE score and Micro Satellite Instability (MSI) scores of the high-risk group were significantly higher relative to those of the low-risk group. The dysfunction and exclusion scores of different validation groups were significantly different between the high and low-risk groups, but the trends were opposite (Fig. 7a, b).

sec.title: Immunological features and immune checkpoint associated with the risk score
sec.p: The aforementioned results confirmed the ability of the risk score to predict the response of patients to immunotherapy. To further examine the immune characteristics and the specific immune checkpoints associated with the risk score, immune infiltration and correlation analyses for common immune checkpoints were performed for different risk groups. The immune infiltration results in the training group revealed that the expression of T cells CD4 memory resting, T cells regulatory (Treg-s), monocytes, dendritic cells resting, mast cells resting, and eosinophils were higher in the low-risk group. In comparison, the expression of T cells CD4 memory activated, T cells gamma delta, natural killer (NK) cells resting, macrophages M0, macrophages M1, and the mast cells activated were higher in the high-risk group (Fig. 8a). Similar findings were obtained in the validation group (Fig. 8b). In the training group, among the 47 common immune checkpoints, 33 were significantly different between the high and low-risk groups; 31 were correlated with the risk score, among which 5 were positively correlated and 26 were negatively correlated (Fig. 9a). In the validation group, 25 markers were significantly different between the different risk groups. Additionally, 26 markers were found to be correlated with the risk score, with 18 showing a positive correlation and 8 showing a negative correlation (Fig. 9b).

sec.title: The risk score is capable of predicting treatment efficacy
sec.p: To further explore the clinical utility of the risk scores, we performed a drug sensitivity analysis using the DEGs in the high and low-risk groups. The results showed that, among the 198 antitumor compounds, 97 were detected in the training group, and 155 in the validation group were significantly different between the high and low-risk groups. The median IC50 values for the top 10 antitumor drugs with the most pronounced differences between the risk groups in the training cohort were presented. The findings demonstrated that the IC50 values for these drugs were significantly lower in the low-risk group (Fig. 10a). Consistent results were observed in the validation cohort (Fig. 10b). Detailed information about these top 10 antitumor compounds is provided in Table 2.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: LUAD is a major public health concern worldwide [2]. Although new treatment methods are continuously being developed to prolong the survival period of patients, the disease remains difficult to control [3, 4]. Unlike the lipid droplets, the correlation between mitochondria and tumors has been extensively studied. Several drugs targeting mitochondria, such as Enasidenib, Ivosidenib, and Rampamycin, have been designed, but their clinical efficacy has not been validated [30–33]. Lipid droplets, as organelles with the functions of storing and transferring energy, play an important role in the development of tumors [14, 15]. In the tumor tissues, the lipid droplets provide the energy needed for rapid proliferation of tumor cells and phospholipid membranes required for the synthesis of endomembrane organelles [16, 34, 35]. Interestingly, there is a close connection between these two energy metabolism organelles. Studies have found that there are two types of contact between lipid droplets and mitochondria: dynamic and stable anchoring, both of which participate in energy transfer [36, 37]. In addition, lipid droplets can regulate mitochondria via the Peroxisome Proliferator-Activated Receptor Gamma Coactivator 1-Alpha (PGC-1α) via Adipose Triglyceride Lipase (ATGL) [12, 38, 39]. Recently, Mingqi Han et.al discovered a subtle relationship between lipid droplets and mitochondria, which is crucial in tumor metabolism and survival [19]. However, the role of LMRGs in LUAD has not been clarified. In this study, we screened for the LMRGs that are strongly related to the survival of LUAD.

Firstly, we obtained RNA-seq data of LUAD, lipid Droplet genes, and Mitochondrial genes from public databases. A series of differential analyses, intersection analyses, univariate COX regression, LASSO regression, and multivariate COX regression were conducted, which identified 8 key LMRGs in LUAD. These genes were then utilized to develop a risk score model. Next, patients were divided into high and low-risk groups according to the median of the risk score. In the risk model, ABLIM3, AK4, CAV2, CPS1, CYP24A1, and DLGAP5 were risk factors, while FGR and SH3BP5 were protective factors. In addition, we compared the expression of the 8 key LMGs among different groups. The analysis revealed that the expression patterns of ABLIM3 and CAV2 varied in different groups and were inconsistent with their expected roles in the model. Previous studies have shown that ABLIM3 primarily binds to actin to facilitate adhesion and improve the cytoskeleton, however, its function in tumors is unclear [40]. Other studies have demonstrated that CAV2 has both inhibitory and promoting effects on cancer [41]. This may explain the observed contradiction. The expression of the other 6 key LMGs was consistent with the current research. Previous studies showed that AK4 is a potential biomarker for lung cancer metastasis. Its overexpression promotes lung cancer metastasis by enhancing Hypoxia-inducible Factor 1(HIF-1) stability and Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) under hypoxic conditions [42]. Furthermore, AK4 is regulated by stress, hypoxia tolerance, and cancer progression, and plays a role in ATP regulation. It is also implicated in the development of tumor drug resistance [43, 44]. Overexpression of DLGAP5 is commonly detected in LUAD and is associated with major driver gene mutations in LUAD, poor prognosis, high IC50 values of commonly used anti-LUAD drugs, increased immune infiltration, and elevated genes associated with immune checkpoint blocking [45]. Moreover, DLGAP5 can modulate cell proliferation, migration, invasion, the cell cycle, and tumor progression via the JAK2/STAT3 signaling pathway [46, 47]. Overexpression of CPS1 has been associated with rapid tumor cell proliferation, and research by Melissa Owusu-Ansah et al. identified elevated CPS1 expression in lung adenocarcinoma samples [48, 49]. The expression of CYP24A1 influences the progression of tumors and the emergence of drug resistance, making it a potential molecular marker for cancer treatment [46]. For the FGR and SH3BP, studies have shown that FGR is a novel target for suppressing ovarian cancer metastasis [49], and high expression of SH3BP5 inhibits the invasion ability of LUAD [50].

After validating the risk score model’s performance, we analyzed the biological functions and potential signaling pathways associated with different genes across the risk groups. The results indicated that these differentially expressed genes are primarily involved in mitosis and the cell cycle, with the risk score showing a significant positive correlation with most aspects of the cell cycle. Correlation analysis showed that cell cycle checkpoints were the most highly enriched. Disruptions in the cell cycle have been associated with tumor development and poor prognosis. Tumor cells accumulate mutations that impair the balance between mitotic and anti-mitotic signaling, leading to uncontrolled proliferation. Chromosome instability is also commonly detected in tumors, and cell cycle checkpoints are utilized to evaluate the normal progression of the cell cycle[51]. This implies that LMGs can regulate chromosome mitosis, cell cycle, and cell cycle checkpoints in tumors, and disruption of this regulation leads to the proliferation of tumor cells. Currently, inhibitors targeting the cell cycle checkpoints have been reported, such as CDK inhibitors [51], and our results provide a new perspective to the development of targeted cell cycle therapy based on lipid drop-mitochondria.

Next, we explored the prediction performance of the risk score in patients receiving clinical immunotherapy. As we know, immunotherapy has improved the treatment of patients with advanced lung cancer [52]. However, how to more easily determine whether patients respond to immunotherapy is an issue that warrants further investigation. IPS is a scoring scheme developed by Pornpimol Charoentong et al. for predicting the therapeutic effect of immune checkpoint inhibitors [52]. A higher score indicates higher sensitivity to immune checkpoint inhibitors and better therapeutic effect. TIDE is another analytical tool for assessing the efficacy of immunotherapy. It evaluates the immune escape by calculating the interactions between tumor cells, immune cells, and immune escape mechanisms [53]. A higher TIDE score indicates a poorer response to immunotherapy. Given that the LUAD data for the training group was sourced from the TCGA database, we were able to directly utilize the IPS data from the TCIA database [24, 25]. The analysis revealed that the low-risk group demonstrated a greater sensitivity to immunotherapy compared to the high-risk group. To validate these findings, we analyzed the training and validation cohorts using the IOBR package. When combined with the TIDE results, the data suggest that the low-risk group may experience more favorable outcomes from immunotherapy. Moreover, we analyzed and compared the immune cell infiltration profiles between the different risk groups. The results showed that more resting-type immune cells, such as T cells CD4 memory resting and mast cells resting, were highly expressed in the low-risk group, while activated-type immune cells, such as T cells CD4 memory activated and mast cells activated, were highly expressed in the high-risk group. Previous investigations have demonstrated that, although immune cells can identify and destroy nascent tumor cells in a cancer immunosurveillance process under physiological conditions, tumors may be influenced by diverse factors [54]. Immune cells may act as guardians (antitumor immunity) or bystanders or supporters of tumors (tumor-promoting immunity), making them a “double-edged sword” in the tumor microenvironment [54, 55]. Therefore, we analyzed the relationship between common immune checkpoints and risk scores. Although some discrepancies were noted between the training and validation groups, significant differences in the expression of most immune checkpoint genes were observed across the different risk groups. These inconsistencies may stem from variations in tumor staging across the datasets. Further investigation with a larger sample size is required to clarify these differences.

Finally, we explored the performance of the risk score model in predicting response to anticancer drugs. In the training group, the drug sensitivity analysis indicated that the low-risk group was more sensitive to the top 10 drugs. With the exception of Uprosertib, the remaining drugs were also evaluated in the validation group. Although most of these drugs are not yet approved for clinical use, preliminary research has been conducted on them. For example, BMS-754807, an inhibitor of insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF1R), demonstrates a synergistic effect by disrupting the cell cycle and interacting with other anticancer agents, such as dasatinib and 2-deoxyglucose, thereby enhancing its antitumor efficacy [56–59]. A study indicated that combining the Aurora B inhibitor ZM447439 with the IGF1R inhibitor OSI-906 could suppress cell proliferation by disrupting chromosome alignment and spindle assembly checkpoints. However, research on the use of these inhibitors in tumors remains limited, and further studies are necessary to confirm their antitumor efficacy [60]. Inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase 3β (GSK3β) by SB216763 was demonstrated to significantly decrease the proliferation of glioblastoma cells and induce apoptosis of glioblastoma cells. In addition, it prevented the proliferation of prostate cancer cells [61, 62]. Although the effect of the ROCK inhibitor GSK269962A on LUAD has not been reported, it can inhibit the proliferation and cell death of melanoma cells in vitro [63]. Doramapimod can inhibit the phosphorylated p-38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p-38-MAPK) pathway, thereby preventing the proliferation of non-small cell lung cancer cells [64]. In addition, it can reverse the resistance to vinorelbine [65]. Oxaliplatin is often used to treat digestive tract tumors. Previously, oxaliplatin-loaded drug-eluting beads transarterial chemoembolization was found to be a safe and effective treatment for patients with unresectable or advanced lung cancer [66]. It has also been reported that WZ4003 increases the sensitivity of non-small cell lung cancer cells to gefitinib by inhibiting activin receptor-like kinase 5 (ARK5) and epithelial-mesenchymal transition [67]. However, compared to the previous drugs, PRT062607 and JAK1_8709 have not been extensively investigated in solid tumors. Although the drugs identified by this risk score model currently lack extensive clinical data and have unclear safety profiles, which limits their immediate clinical application, the model provides significant theoretical insights for guiding future research.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This study has some strengths that need to be acknowledged. Firstly, we integrated the lipid drop gene and mitochondrial gene to construct the LD-M risk score model, which exhibited good prediction performance for the prognosis of LUAD. Secondly, our study presents a simpler method for predicting the risk values. Finally, this risk prediction model can help clinicians predict the efficacy of clinical immunotherapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapy in patients with LUAD. However, we did not perform experimental verification to confirm our findings. This is because the expression level of most genes used in the model has been confirmed in LUAD. In the future, researchers should verify our results in larger clinical samples, to enhance the clinical application of the model. In addition, we used currently available datasets which may not contain all relevant genes. Thus, additional genes need to be explored in further studies.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: A risk score for LUAD including eight LMGs: ABLIM3, AK4, CAV2, CPS1, CYP24A1, DLGAP5, FGR, and SH3BP5, was constructed in this study. The risk score was highly correlated with the cell cycle genes. Patients in the low-risk group were likely to experience better therapeutic outcomes. Additionally, these patients demonstrated greater sensitivity to anti-tumor agents such as BMS-754807, ZM447439, SB216763, GSK269962A, doramapimod, oxaliplatin, and WZ4003 compared to those in the high-risk group. In summary, our LD-M risk score model offers valuable insights for tailoring individualized treatment strategies in LUAD.
